summary: Proposes the Address plus Port approach to the IPv4 address shortage, in which several hosts share one IPv4 address by each being given a distinct range of port numbers. This avoids giving every host a unique global IPv4 address. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Address plus Port (A+P) lets several customers share a public IPv4 address by giving each a different range of ports. Tunnels and signaling help route packets to the customer assigned that range.

questions: what is a+p address plus port
how does a+p differ from carrier grade nat
what is a port range router
how does stateless a+p mapping work
subtitle: An experimental method for sharing IPv4 addresses by assigning customers separate port ranges.

tldr.problem: Providers may not have enough public IPv4 addresses to assign a unique address to every customer.
tldr.mechanism: Address plus Port (A+P) treats port-number bits as part of an extended address, assigning each customer a shared IPv4 address and a port range.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes an Experimental architecture with tunneling, optional NAT, and signaling; it is not an Internet Standards Track specification.

today: RFC 6346 is Experimental, published for examination, implementation, and evaluation. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Sharing Addresses Without a Core NAT
sections.content:
RFC 6346 proposes A+P to address IPv4 exhaustion while IPv6 is not yet widely deployed enough to replace IPv4. It treats some TCP or UDP port bits as part of an extended IPv4 address, allowing multiple customers to share one public IPv4 address with distinct port ranges.

The RFC argues that translation should remain as close to the customer as possible so customers retain control. It describes concerns with Carrier Grade NATs, including application restrictions, state management, and possible single points of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Several customers can share one public IPv4 address if each receives a different port range. A+P is designed to let customers control any translation rather than relying only on a provider's core NAT.

sections.title: The Three A+P Functions
sections.content:
The architecture separates encapsulation and decapsulation, NAT, and signaling. A Port-Range Router (PRR) forwards A+P packets, often through a tunnel. NAT supports legacy hosts that assume they have a full address. Signaling tells devices their address, port range, lifetime, tunnel information, and whether NAT is available.

Multiple authenticated gateways may form an A+P subsystem. A gateway can delegate part of its address-and-port space to another gateway, and packets can be translated at the customer device or at a provider-side NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: A+P has separate roles for tunneling, translation, and allocation signaling. The network uses the destination port range to direct packets to the gateway responsible for it.

sections.title: Stateless Mapping and IPv6 Tunnels
sections.content:
Stateless A+P Mapping (SMAP) encapsulates IPv4 packets in IPv6 packets and can recover them at the other endpoint. IPv6 addresses are constructed from IPv4 address and port information with a provisioned IPv6 prefix. The RFC identifies 64:ff9b::/96 as a possible well-known prefix.

Stateless mapping does not keep per-flow state, while binding-table mode uses a table to associate a shared IPv4 address and port range with an IPv6 address. The RFC says dynamic port allocation is supported in binding-table mode, not stateless mode. SMAP can carry IPv4 service across IPv6-only network segments.
sections.plainLanguage: SMAP wraps IPv4 packets in IPv6 packets for transport between gateways. It can calculate the mapping directly or use a table that records address and port assignments.

sections.title: Port Allocation and Packet Handling
sections.content:
Providers may assign an initial port range and later allocate additional ranges. The RFC gives 128 ports as an initial example and describes limits on how quickly a customer can request more ranges to reduce request storms.

On incoming traffic, a PRR checks the destination address and port. It tunnels packets for delegated ranges to the matching customer gateway, passes NAT-managed traffic to the NAT function, and discards packets with no matching assignment. ICMP requires special handling, and a PRR may need to reassemble fragments to inspect destination ports.
sections.plainLanguage: A PRR checks the destination port to decide which tunnel or NAT should receive a packet. Customers may request more ports, subject to provider limits.

sections.title: Limitations and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Customers sharing one IPv4 address cannot both offer a service on the same port, such as port 80. Some applications that require well-known ports may need to adapt. Port translation also has the IPsec compatibility issues associated with NAT.

The RFC says A+P can reduce logging from per-connection mappings to occasional port-range allocations, depending on where NAT is placed. It presents this as a trade-off affecting scalability and privacy, not as a new security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing an address means customers cannot use the same port for separate services. The RFC also compares the logging needed for A+P with per-connection NAT mappings.
